conditions: Give the Armament line an explicit option for a pair of weapons, or declare that any further weapon or a shield beyond the chosen option is free fiction and sits outside the kit budget.

Reconcile all nine class starting kits and all nine character-creation exemplar loadout blocks with whatever the kit model is made to say; they are the binding counter-example, not the equipment chapter.
Decide the case in which one object falls under two lines at different prices (a bow reads as both ranged and two-handed), so the kit can be costed without consulting per-item data.
Preserve the existing class-kit exemption from Discipline prerequisites when the Armament line is touched.
Reject any submission that relies on the fabricated ranged starting kit line; the real ranged kit carries a shortbow and no shield.
point_of_contention: Do the four category-based kit lines fully express what the legacy named-weapon catalog expressed, such that the catalog can be withdrawn without any change to the kit model itself?
reasoning: Three of the refuting arguments survived and none was answered by a counter-example. The counter-example drawn from the book's own builds held up on inspection: four kits out of the nine hand a hero a pair or a triple of weapons (a blade pair, a bow beside a dagger, a one-handed weapon alongside a two-handed one and a shield, and a double-dagger set), and a shield is bundled by exactly one Armament option, so those loadouts have no row to occupy. The point that leftover points convert only into packs also held, so there is no priced route to a second weapon. The second refute's broader counts (nine named kit lines and nine exemplar blocks that reuse them with no kit-point accounting) also stood. The one support argument on this topic is scoped to the direction of the deletion rather than to kit completeness, so it does not rescue the completeness claim and offers no counter-example against it. Two fact-checks matter. First, the Armament line's genuinely expressible property set is the two-handed case only, and the count of card tags (eight total tags, of which five are armament-or-shield categories) is consistent between the competing speakers rather than in dispute. Second, the integrity warning was confirmed: the quoted ranged starting kit containing a longbow, a shield and a quiver does not exist in the book, and the ranged class's real line carries a shortbow with no shield, so any conclusion resting on that quotation is unsupported.
ruling: The council must treat the category kit as an incomplete substitute, not a complete one. Five mutually exclusive Armament options cannot record a loadout carrying two weapons, cannot price an object that qualifies under two different lines, and carry no item-level property, attack-mode or range value. Withdrawing the catalog therefore cannot be a pure deletion of tables: the Armament line must be extended or an explicit rule must declare extra carried weapons to be free fiction outside the budget, and the class kit lists and character-creation exemplars must be reconciled to whatever the kit can actually say.

conditions: State a destination for the object-to-property mapping, the per-item range bands, and the per-item Discipline entry requirements before deleting the rows that carry them.
Keep the property rules that already survive item-independently, but re-author the definitions so they no longer establish their scope by enumerating rows that will no longer exist.
Author one slot value per armour weight class, or print the slot cost on the Covering line; the current spread across medium and heavy rows cannot be derived from the weight class.
Decide the fate of the gear notes and their item-level damage numbers explicitly; do not let them contradict the rule that a kit grants no damage.
Edit the reference-sheet reprint in the same change as the chapter, since it duplicates the property cells and the slot values.
Do not assume a pre-existing card field will absorb the residue; the supplied chapters show no such field.
point_of_contention: Is the mechanical content carried by the named tables already reproducible from the surviving kit, tag and prose surfaces, so that deletion can proceed without a destination plan?
reasoning: Three of the four positions on this topic refuted the no-residue premise, and the lone support position concedes that no counter-example was found for either the weapon properties or the armour slot column, supporting only the identity half of the gear family and expressly not its mechanics. The disagreements were largely about size, not existence, and the fact-checks settle the size. What genuinely survives: the Finesse substitution is stated twice as a rule of how damage resolves, with no item list attached, and one of those statements credits a class feature with extending it beyond any single weapon; the two-handed case's two-slot cost is repeated by item type in the encumbrance section; and the general encumbrance rule gives armour a band rather than a per-row value. What does not survive: the ten property-bearing weapon rows and the reprint that repeats them, the per-item range column, and the Discipline-requirement column exist only in those tables. I settle the Light dispute: the Light tag has no consumer procedure anywhere in the nine chapters, only its own definition plus one charge-rule aside and one buckler note that assume two-weapon fighting exists, so the claim that it has no consumer procedure is correct while the stronger claim that it has no consumer at all is not. I settle the property-burden dispute the other way in part: the burden is smaller than the largest framing, because the two-handed case is category-expressible and separately restated, one property carries no number and applies to a single item, and another has no procedure; but four properties do carry live numbers whose item assignment or band exists nowhere else. On armour slots the count correction is right and the larger count is wrong: the eight rows hold three distinct slot values, not four, and both the medium and heavy classes split across two values each, so no weight-class rule reproduces the column. On gear, the pack layer overlaps the catalog on object identities but carries neither the slot numbers nor the notes-column rules, and several notes state item damage numbers that sit awkwardly against the chapter's own statement that a kit grants no damage. Finally, the claim that a ready-made card field already exists to receive this content is not supported by the nine chapters: no card table in them carries a range or keyword field.
ruling: The council must treat the residue as real but mixed, and must treat deletion as more than a single-file editorial change. Part of what the tables carry is already stated item-independently elsewhere and survives removal; the remainder does not. No surviving surface reproduces the mapping from a specific object to its properties, its range band, its Discipline entry requirement, its armour slot value, or the rules that the gear catalog attaches to items by name. Those items must have a stated destination before, or in the same change as, the rows that carry them.

conditions: Adjudicate the Disciplines gate explicitly: either state that Disciplines gate cards and not gear, or give the armour tables a real requirement column so the asserted value has a home.
Resolve every item-named consumer outside the equipment chapter, including the class kits, the creation exemplars, the magic-item types, the bestiary attack lines and the glossary headwords.
Treat the third Armor, third Heavy Weapon and Axes ranks as a balance decision with an owner, not as decoration to be deleted.
Edit the reference sheet in the same change; it reprints the catalog and its gating column.
Preserve the mounts, vehicles and the mounted-combat and chase rules, which carry no permission gate and have no other home.
Record that the quoted ranged starting kit line containing a longbow, a shield and a quiver is not in the book; no strand analysis may depend on it.
point_of_contention: Are the consequences of withdrawing the named catalog contained within the equipment chapter, or does the removal strand rules and named references in other chapters that must be adjudicated first?
reasoning: The enumerating finding survived on its own instrumented counts, and the gate finding was not rebutted at all. The fact-checks confirm both. Class starting kits and creation exemplars equip named objects; magic-item type fields and bestiary attack lines are keyed to catalog names; the reference sheet reprints the whole catalog as a second deletion surface, including a shield table that does tab a Discipline requirement. The gate finding is the sharper one and it checks out: the Disciplines chapter names a heavy armour requirement at the third Armor rank and sends the reader to two chapters whose armour tables are built from name, weight class, damage reduction and slots and contain no Discipline column at all, so the asserted value is verifiable nowhere; that rank string occurs exactly once across the nine chapters, while the weapon gate is tabbed in both weapon-table copies and the shield gate in the reference sheet, so the register is asymmetric. The enumerating finding's dead-rank cases also check out in substance: the third Armor rank and the third Heavy Weapon rank are demanded only by that armour sentence and by the maul rows respectively, and the Axes ranks are consumed only by the three named axe rows, which makes those ranks a balance question rather than residue to be swept away. Consistency matters here as well: the same chapter that asserts an equipment gate elsewhere releases class kit gear from prerequisites, so the book currently carries two permission models and the purge must say which one survives.
ruling: The council must treat the consequences as cross-chapter and partly unadjudicated. Withdrawal strands item-named consumers in the class, character-creation, magic-item, bestiary, glossary and reference-sheet chapters, and it collides with a live contradiction already in the book: the Disciplines chapter asserts an armour entry requirement that no armour table records. That contradiction must be decided explicitly as part of the removal, not inherited silently, and the ranks that only a named item currently justifies call for a balance decision of their own instead of being swept away with the rows.
